title: Hawkins v. McGee
summary: A surgeon’s specific guarantee may be a contractual promise. The remedy measures the promised hand against the hand actually delivered.
notes:
Court: Supreme Court of New Hampshire (1929).

Reading distinction: the casebook uses the same case to introduce both the identification of an enforceable promise and the expectation measure. Contractual liability for a promised result and negligence in providing medical care are separate questions. The surrounding notes ask how later medical-promise formalities and the context of reassurance affect enforcement; they are not part of this case’s holding.

sections.Parties: George Hawkins, the patient, sued Dr. McGee, the surgeon. The defendant challenged the contract claim and the damages instructions.
sections.Material Facts: Hawkins had a scarred right hand from an electrical burn suffered years earlier. McGee solicited the operation and grafted skin from Hawkins’s chest onto the hand. Hawkins offered evidence of a guarantee of a “hundred per cent perfect” or “hundred per cent good” hand. Hair grew on the graft. Statements predicting a three- or four-day hospital stay and an early return to work were also in evidence.
sections.Procedural History: The casebook splits one decision into a liability excerpt and a damages excerpt. In the first, the court treats the guarantee as evidence that could go to a jury, while treating the recovery-time statements as estimates. In the later excerpt, it rejects the trial court’s damages instruction and orders a new trial. The assigned text does not establish a final recovery after that new trial.
sections.Issue: Could the surgeon’s words reasonably amount to a promise of a specified result, and how should damages for its breach be measured?
sections.Holding: The asserted guarantee could support a contract finding. Damages are the difference between the value of the hand as promised and its value as delivered, together with qualifying incidental consequences. Ordinary pain inherent in the contemplated operation is excluded from that calculation.
sections.Reasoning: The court first decides whether words can reasonably bear the alleged contractual meaning; where they can, the jury determines whether they were used and understood that way. The surgeon’s solicitation and interest in undertaking the operation give context to the guarantee. The damages comparison places Hawkins in the position successful performance would have produced. Ordinary operative pain was part of the performance Hawkins agreed to undergo, rather than an additional loss caused by failure to produce the promised result. Worsening is already captured in the difference between the actual and promised hand and should not be counted twice.
